ClarityCheck 是一款人臉辨識工具，很難想像它有甚麼正當用途。據報該工具發生重大私隱外洩事件，導致數以百萬計的臉部相片在互聯網上公開曝光。

絕大多數受害者很可能完全不知道自己的相片已被上載到該網站，亦從未就此給予同意……

This service lets anyone upload a photo of someone and run a reverse search to identify them across platforms like social media. Although ClarityCheck requires users to agree that they have the rights to the uploaded image, security researcher Jeremiah Fowler told Wired he is extremely skeptical of that.

The site's blog includes posts such as 'How to Find Someone on Dating Sites by Email' and 'How to Find Someone on Hinge (Even Without a Match)'.

Farrell told ExpressCheck that more than nine million image files uploaded to ClarityCheck were left publicly exposed on a cloud server for months, noting that the files were predominantly facial images, with some cropped and resized duplicates also included.

I recently discovered a publicly exposed database that was not password-protected or encrypted. It contained approximately 9,042,977 image files, totalling 450.2GB. The exposed records were primarily facial images, stored in folders labelled 'faces' and 'profiles'. During my investigation, I reviewed a sampling of the exposed images, which included facial photos of adults, teenagers, and children… The large number of uploaded images I saw could have come from third-party sources, such as private archives, social media accounts, dating app profiles, screenshots, or physical photos uploaded by other users.

He traced the database back and confirmed it belonged to ClarityCheck, which acknowledged owning the data and said it had now been secured.

9to5Mac's Take

One risk Fowler raised is that the photos and associated identity data could be exploited by scammers to craft fake social media posts aimed at deceiving the victims' family and friends. A fairly common scam involves impersonating a family member in an urgent situation and demanding an immediate wire transfer. With facial photos in hand, these types of fraud would undoubtedly become easier to pull off.
